part2.intro: Three young people write about their best day out.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Tuan
texts.text: For my thirteenth birthday, my parents took me to see a musical at the big theatre in the city. We sat in the front row, so I could see everything. The singing was amazing, and at the end the actors came out and talked to us. Before the show, we had dinner at a small Vietnamese restaurant nearby. My dad said it was the best noodle soup he'd ever had!

texts.label: B
texts.title: Grace
texts.text: Last spring my family stayed at a hotel in the mountains for two nights. My grandparents paid for the trip as a present for my mum's birthday. The hotel had an indoor swimming pool and a games room, so my brother and I were never bored. The only problem was the weather – it rained every day, so we couldn't go walking. I'd still like to go back next year.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Marco
texts.text: My best day out was a cooking class at an Italian restaurant in town. My friend Leo won two places in a competition and invited me. The chef taught us to make pizza and fresh pasta. It was harder than I thought, and my first pizza was a bit black! But we ate everything at the end. Now I cook dinner for my family every Sunday.

items.q: Who went somewhere because of a prize?
Who had a meal before the main activity of the day?
Who says the weather spoiled part of the trip?
Who now does something new at home?
Who met some performers?
Whose day out was a present for someone else?
Who did something wrong the first time they tried?

part3.title: The bike doctor
part3.text:
When fourteen-year-old Jamal Hussain's bike broke last year, he didn't have enough money to take it to a shop. "The man at the bike shop said it would cost forty pounds," he says. "So I decided to repair it myself."

Jamal watched videos online and borrowed some tools from his grandfather, who used to work at a car garage. "Grandad helped me a lot at the beginning. He showed me how to use the tools properly." After three weekends, the bike was working again.

Soon Jamal's friends started bringing him their bikes. Then the neighbours did the same. Now Jamal has his own small business in his grandfather's garage. He opens on Saturday mornings and usually repairs four or five bikes a day. "I'm not as fast as a real mechanic," he says, "but I'm getting better."

Jamal charges much less than the shops – usually five or ten pounds. "I don't want to get rich. I just enjoy it. And people are always happy when they ride away on their bikes."

His parents were worried at first. "My mum thought I wouldn't have time for my homework," says Jamal. "But I only work on Saturdays, and my school marks are still good."

Next year, Jamal wants to give free lessons at the sports centre to teach other teenagers how to look after their bikes. "Everyone should know how to repair a tyre," he says.

items.q: Why did Jamal decide to repair his bike himself?
options: He wanted to learn something new.
A repair at the shop cost too much for him.

items.q: How did Jamal's grandfather help him?
options: He bought him some new tools.
He taught him how to use the tools.

items.q: What does Jamal say about his work?
options: He works more slowly than an expert.

He opens his garage every day.

items.q: Why was Jamal's mother worried?
options: She thought he would hurt himself.
She thought he would have no time for school work.
She didn't want strangers to come to the house.

part4.title: The first cinemas
part4.text:
The first films were made in the 1890s. At that time there were no cinemas, so people {19} to theatres, cafés and even tents at country fairs to see them. The films were very short – often less than a minute – and they had no sound.

In 1905, the first real cinema {20} in the city of Pittsburgh in the USA. It was called the Nickelodeon, because a ticket {21} just five cents, or a 'nickel'. It was very popular, and soon there were thousands of cinemas across the country.

In the 1920s and 1930s, cinemas became huge, beautiful buildings, with seats for more than 2,000 people. Because the films had no sound, a musician often {22} the piano during the film. Going to the cinema every week was a big {23} for many families.

Today lots of people watch films at home, but cinemas are still popular. Many people still go there to {24} the latest films on a really big screen.

part7.model: Last Friday Sam and his parents had dinner at a restaurant for his birthday. The food was delicious. When the waiter brought the bill, Dad looked for his wallet, but he couldn't find it. He left it at home! Luckily, Sam had his birthday money in his pocket, so he paid for dinner.

items.q: Where is the girl's mum now?

script.t: Dad, where's Mum? Is she still at the bank?
No, she finished there an hour ago.
So is she at the library? She wanted to get a new book.
She was going to go there, but it's closed today. She's at the post office now, sending a parcel to Aunt Mai.

items.q: How much does the girl pay to go into the museum?

script.t: Excuse me, how much is it to get into the science museum?
It's eight pounds for adults.
I'm fourteen. Is it cheaper for children?
Yes, under-sixteens pay six pounds. It's only four pounds on Wednesdays, but today's Saturday, I'm afraid.
That's OK. One ticket, please.

items.q: What's the matter with the boy?

script.t: Hello, Ben. What's the problem today? Is it your cold again?
No, doctor, that's much better now. I hurt my foot playing football yesterday.
I see. Does your head hurt too?
A little, but that's only because I didn't sleep well.
OK, let me look at your foot.

items.q: What time does the swimming pool close today?

script.t: Let's go swimming after school today. The pool closes at eight, doesn't it?
Only in summer. In winter it closes at seven.
OK, so we've got lots of time.
Not today. Today it closes at six, because there's a swimming competition in the evening. We'll have to go straight after school.

items.q: Where are the friends going to have lunch?

script.t: I'm hungry. Shall we go to that Italian restaurant?
It's a bit expensive. What about the café in the park?
It's closed in the winter. Let's just go back to my house – my dad's making soup.
Even better!

part2.intro: You will hear a hotel manager talking to a group of students on a school trip.
part2.title: Park View Hotel

items.label: Breakfast for school groups starts at:
The swimming pool is on floor:

script.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Park View Hotel. I hope you had a good journey. I'm the hotel manager, and I'm going to tell you a few important things. First, breakfast. It's in the restaurant on the ground floor. For most guests it starts at seven o'clock, but for school groups it's at half past seven, so please don't come down earlier. We also have a lovely swimming pool. It isn't in the basement like in a lot of hotels – it's on the second floor, next to the gym. You can use it from four until eight every evening. Your teachers tell me you're going to visit the city museum on Tuesday and the castle on Wednesday. The tourist bus stops right outside the hotel, so it's very easy. If you have any problems with your room, please talk to our receptionist, Mr Ruiz. That's R-U-I-Z. He speaks Spanish and English. And finally, please be careful with your room keys. If you lose one, you'll have to pay fifteen pounds for a new one. Have a great stay!

items.q: When does Chloe work at the café?

What is Max going to do?
options: ask for a job at the café
visit Chloe at work on Sunday
try to get a job at the cinema

script.t: Hi Chloe. I heard you've got a job at the café in the high street. Is that right?
Yes! I started two weeks ago. I wanted to work on Saturday mornings, but another girl already does that. So I work on Sunday afternoons, from twelve until five.
Cool. Do you cook?
No, I'm not allowed to cook yet. I thought I'd be in the kitchen washing plates all day, but they have a machine for that. I take people's orders and bring the food to their tables.
Do you like it?
I love it. The money isn't much – five pounds an hour. I get a free lunch, which is nice. But the best thing is the other waiters. They're really funny and we laugh all afternoon.
What are you going to do with the money? Buy clothes?
My friends spend their money on clothes and concert tickets, but I'm saving it. My cousin and I want to go to Paris in the summer, and I have to pay for my train ticket.
That sounds great. Maybe I could ask for a job at the café too!
They don't need anyone at the moment. But the cinema next door is looking for someone to sell tickets at the weekend.
Really? I'll go there this afternoon and ask.
Good luck! And come and have a hot chocolate at the café one Sunday.
Not this Sunday – I've got a football match. But soon!

items.q: Why is she phoning?

script.t: Hello. My name's Helen Ward. I've got a room at your hotel for Friday and Saturday night.
Yes, Mrs Ward, I can see your booking here.
The problem is, I can't come on Friday now because of my work. Could I have the room for Saturday and Sunday night instead?
Let me check. Yes, that's fine.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking about a visit to the dentist.
items.q: How did he feel after the visit?

script.t: I went to the dentist this morning. I was really scared before I went, because last time it hurt a lot. We had to wait twenty minutes, but I didn't mind – I read a comic. The dentist was really kind, and she said my teeth were perfect, so she didn't need to do anything! I was so happy when I came out.

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a film they saw at the cinema.
items.q: What did the girl think of the film?
options: The story was hard to follow.

script.t: So what did you think of the film?
Well, the actors were good, I suppose, and it wasn't too long.
But?
I didn't understand what was happening half the time. There were too many people in the story, and they kept going to different places!

script.t: Good morning. Would you like a map of the town?
No, thanks, I've already got one. I'm looking for the Grand Hotel. I know it's in Hill Street, but I don't know the number.
It's number forty-two. Would you like to take the bus?
No, I'll walk. Thanks.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking about the new swimming pool in her town.
items.q: What problem does she talk about?
options: It's a long way from her home.

script.t: The new swimming pool in our town is lovely. It's big, the water's warm, and tickets are only two pounds. I thought it would be a long way from my house, but it's only ten minutes on my bike. The only problem is that everyone in town wants to go there! There are so many people in the water that I can hardly swim.

part5.intro: You will hear Hannah talking to her friend Leo about a school project. Which place did each student visit?

script.t: Hi Hannah. How's your project about jobs in our town going?

Great! Each of us visited a different place and talked to someone who works there. Ryan wanted to go to the garage, because he loves cars, but they were too busy. So he went to the hotel by the river and talked to the receptionist.
And Mia? She loves acting.
That's right, so she went to the theatre. She even met one of the actors!
What about Duc? Did he go to the post office? His mum works there.
He thought about it, but in the end he chose the bank. He wants to work with money one day.
And Sophie?
Sophie wanted to visit the café in the park, but it was closed for the week. So she went to the Chinese restaurant in Market Street instead. The cook showed her the kitchen.
Lucky her! And where did you go?
I went to the museum. I talked to a woman who looks after the old paintings. It was really interesting.
It sounds like a great project.
